title: The times that open
hook: in prostration, the last third of the night, between adhan and iqamah, while fasting

segments.voice: Yesterday: ameen, the angel's answer. Ask good for someone absent, and the same is asked for you.

Every office has one. The manager whose door is technically always open, but everyone knows the good time to ask is Friday afternoon, after lunch, when things are calm. Timing isn't everything, but it's something. Du'a can be made anywhere, any time, in any words. That's still true; the door is never locked. But the hadith collections also name certain moments when the door is described as especially wide open. Moments people save their biggest asks for. Today: iqamah.
screen: `THE DOOR IS ALWAYS OPEN.` → `BUT SOME MOMENTS ARE WIDER.` → `WHERE PEOPLE SAVE THEIR BIGGEST ASKS.`

segments.voice: Here are four of them. The first you met on day one hundred five: in prostration. Sahih Muslim reports that the closest a servant is to his Lord is while prostrating, so ask much there. Forehead on the floor, some Muslims pour their private requests into those few seconds, silently, in their own words. The second is the last third of the night. Bukhari and Muslim report that every night, when the last third remains, our Lord descends to the nearest heaven and says: who is calling on Me, that I may answer? Who is asking of Me, that I may give? Who is seeking forgiveness, that I may forgive? Scholars have long differed on how to understand that descent; many simply accept it without asking how. Either way, it's a question asked in the dark while almost everyone sleeps, and it's why some Muslims set an alarm for an hour before dawn. The third is small and ordinary: between the adhan and the iqamah, the call to prayer and the call to stand. Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi report that a du'a made in that gap is not turned back. Those minutes of waiting in the mosque, checking the time, are described as an open door. The fourth is while fasting. Tirmidhi reports that the fasting person's du'a is among those not rejected, and some Muslims make du'a just before breaking the fast at sunset. The hadith name others too, like an hour on Friday and the traveler's du'a. But look at what these four share. Lowered. Awake while others sleep. Waiting. Hungry. A person a little emptier than usual.
screen: `FIRST: IN PROSTRATION.` · `THE LAST THIRD OF THE NIGHT.` · `BETWEEN THE ADHAN AND THE IQAMAH.` · `WHILE FASTING.` · then, large: `A LITTLE EMPTIER THAN USUAL.`

segments.voice: Run through the four in your mind: face on the floor, the quiet hour before dawn, the waiting minutes before a prayer, the last minute of an empty stomach. Choose the one you could actually reach this week, and picture where you'll be. If you pray, decide what you'll ask for when you get there; if not, decide what you'll sit quietly with.

Iqamah, the call to stand for prayer: the gap between it and the adhan is one of the moments the hadith describe as especially open to du'a, along with prostration, the last third of the night, and the fast.
Your line: knock at the open door. It's never locked; some moments it's just wider. That's day one hundred thirty-five.
